526.title: Strong and trustworthy
526.hook: the best to hire is the strong and the trustworthy (28:26)
526.howItsDone: Muslims often cite 28:26 when speaking of hiring, leadership and work ethic, holding that a person given a role should be both capable and trustworthy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, haya', and your line was modesty is a walk. Which room did you walk into slowly, and what did you say plainly? Day five hundred twenty-six.

Every hiring manager has a list. Experience, references, a good interview, a degree from the right place. Musa has none of it. He's a fugitive with no money, no letters, no home, sitting in a stranger's house in Madyan. He has told the old man his whole story, and the old man has said, don't be afraid, you've escaped from the wrongdoing people. Then one of the daughters speaks up and gives him a reference. Her case rests on two words, and she has seen him earn both.

She says to her father, hire him. Pickthall: "the best (man) that thou canst hire is the strong, the trustworthy." In Arabic, al-qawiyy al-amin. Qawiyy is strong, able, capable of the work. Amin is trustworthy, from the same root as amana, a trust, and iman, faith. How does she know? She's seen both with her own eyes. Strength at the well, where he watered a whole flock that had been waiting behind the shepherds. And trustworthiness on the way home. Commentators tell, from a report attributed to 'Umar, that Musa asked her to walk behind him and call out the way, so that he wouldn't be looking at her as she walked. That detail is from commentary, not the verse. But the point stands either way: she'd watched him work, and she'd watched him behave when no one else was looking. Here's why both words matter. Strength without trust is a danger: a capable person you can't rely on. Trust without strength is a disappointment: a good person who can't do the job. The same pair turns up once more, in Surah An-Naml, from an unlikely mouth: a jinn offering to fetch the Queen of Sheba's throne says he is strong and trustworthy for the job. The old man takes his daughter's advice. He offers Musa marriage to one of his daughters, for eight years of work, or ten if he chooses. And Musa answers, whichever term I complete, let there be no injustice to me. A contract made between two people who each had reason to trust the other. A hadith in Bukhari warns that when trust is lost, the Hour is near.
screen: `AL-QAWIYY AL-AMIN.` · `STRENGTH SEEN AT THE WELL.` · `TRUST SEEN ON THE WALK HOME.` · `BOTH, OR NEITHER IS ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: be both at work. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of the work in front of you today, paid or unpaid: a job, a class, a household, caring for someone. Ask two questions honestly. Where am I strong but not quite trustworthy? A corner I cut, a promise I let slide. And where am I trustworthy but not strong? Something I mean well about but haven't learned to do properly. Pick one of the two to work on today. If you pray, you can ask for strength and trust together. The bell holds the time.
Strong and trustworthy. Al-qawiyy al-amin: the daughter's two words for Musa, able to do the work and safe to trust with it. Today's word.
Your line: strong and trustworthy. Today, finish one task completely and well, the kind of job nobody will check. Day five hundred twenty-six.

527.title: Qarun's keys
527.hook: the rich man told not to exult, but to do good as Allah did good to him (28:76–77)
527.carry: do good as good was done
527.howItsDone: Muslims read Qarun's story as a warning against pride in wealth, and often quote 28:77, do good as God has done good to you, when speaking about charity and balance in worldly life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daughter's two words, and your line was strong and trustworthy. Which task did you finish completely, with nobody checking? Day five hundred twenty-seven.

Not the gold. The keys. Al-Qasas tells of a man named Qarun, from Musa's own people, who had so many treasures that the keys alone, the verse says, would have been a heavy load for a band of strong men. A crew of strong backs, bent under keys, just to open the storerooms. The story never says how much gold there was. It measures the wealth by the weight of its keys. And his own people, the verse says, gave him advice.

The advice comes in five parts, and it holds this world and the next together. Don't exult; God doesn't love the exultant. Seek the home of the hereafter with what God has given you. Don't forget your share of this world. And then, Pickthall: "be thou kind even as Allah hath been kind to thee". In Arabic, ahsin kama ahsana Allahu ilayk. Do good as God has done good to you. The word is ihsan, excellence, doing beautifully. Notice: nobody tells him to give it all away. Enjoy your share, they say. Just let the good flow on in the same direction it came to you. And don't spread corruption on the earth. Qarun's answer is the turn of the story. I was given this only because of knowledge I have. It's mine. I earned it. He doesn't deny God exists; he just leaves God out of the account. Then he goes out before his people in all his finery. Some of them sigh: if only we had what Qarun has, he's so fortunate. But those who'd been given knowledge say, woe to you, God's reward is better for whoever believes and does good. And then, the verse says, God caused the earth to swallow him and his house, and no crowd could help him. The next morning, the ones who had envied him the day before are saying: so God gives freely to whom He wills, and holds back. Classical commentators identify Qarun with Korah, whose rebellion in the Book of Numbers also ends with the ground opening. In the story, the keys were never the problem. The problem was believing they were self-made.
screen: `KEYS TOO HEAVY FOR STRONG MEN.` · `DO GOOD AS GOOD WAS DONE TO YOU.` · `I EARNED IT BY MY OWN KNOWLEDGE.` · `THE ENVIERS, THE NEXT MORNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share something of what you own. Sit, and let the breath settle. Look around the room, or picture your home. Count a few things you have that someone gave you, or that came through luck, or timing, or a parent's work. Then pick one thing, or a little money, that you could pass on this week. A coat you don't wear. Books. A tool. A meal paid for. Picture who it goes to. If you pray, you can thank God for what came to you before it goes on. The bell holds the time.
Qarun's keys. The rich man of Al-Qasas, told to do good as good was done to him, who said his wealth was his own doing. Today's word.
Your line: do good as good was done. Today, give away the thing you picked, and don't make a show of it. Day five hundred twenty-seven.

528.title: Left alone to say "we believe"?
528.hook: do people think they will be left to say we believe and not be tested (29:2)
528.howItsDone: Muslims understand trials, hardships and even blessings as tests from God, and many recite 29:2–3 and ask God for steadfastness in times of difficulty.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Qarun's keys, and your line was do good as good was done. What did you pass on, quietly? Day five hundred twenty-eight, and a new surah.

A goldsmith has a lump of metal that looks like gold. It's the right color. It's heavy. The customer swears it's pure. But the goldsmith doesn't take anyone's word for it. She puts it in the crucible and turns up the heat. Whatever isn't gold separates out and burns away, and what's left is what it really was all along. Surah Al-'Ankabut, the Spider, the twenty-ninth, opens with a question that sounds a lot like that crucible.

After the opening letters, alif, lam, mim, the surah asks. Pickthall: "Do men imagine that they will be left (at ease) because they say, We believe, and will not be tested with affliction?" The next verse answers: those before them were tested too, so that God would make known those who are truthful and those who lie. The word for being tested is from the root of fitnah, today's word. In the old Arabic dictionaries, the root's first meaning is exactly the goldsmith's: putting gold or silver into fire to separate the pure from the impure. From there it spread. Fitnah came to mean a trial, a test, a temptation that pulls at you, and in other places, turmoil and civil strife, the times when a whole community is put through the fire. The Qur'an even calls wealth and children a fitnah, a test. So the test isn't only the hard thing. It can be the good thing, too: what you do with it. Tradition places this surah in Mecca, at a time when the early Muslims were being pressured, some tortured, for their faith. The verse doesn't promise them comfort. It tells them this is what faith is like. Saying we believe is the first step; the fire shows what it's made of. A hadith in Tirmidhi says the people most severely tested are the prophets, then those most like them, and that a person is tested according to the strength of their faith. Read that way, a test is not a punishment and not a sign of being forgotten. In the Qur'an's picture, the crucible is a way of being taken seriously.
screen: `LEFT TO SAY WE BELIEVE?` · `FITNAH: GOLD IN THE FIRE.` · `TRIAL, TEMPTATION, TURMOIL.` · `TESTED AS FAITH IS STRONG.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice today's small test. Sit, and let the breath settle. Run through the day ahead, or the day behind. Where did something push on what you say you believe? A moment of impatience, a chance to cut a corner, a bit of gossip you could join, a good thing that might make you proud. Don't judge it. Just see it clearly, as a goldsmith looks at what comes out of the fire. Name it to yourself: that was the test. If you pray, you can ask to be steady through it. The bell holds the time.
Fitnah. A trial: from a root meaning to put gold in the fire, then any test, temptation or turmoil that shows what faith is made of. Today's word.
Your line: faith is tested. Today, when the small test you noticed comes round again, pause for one breath before you choose. Day five hundred twenty-eight.

529.title: The spider's house
529.hook: the frailest of houses is the spider's (29:41)
529.howItsDone: Muslims read the parable of the spider's house as a reminder to rely on God rather than on idols, wealth or status, and the surah is named Al-'Ankabut for this verse.

segments.voice: Yesterday, fitnah, and your line was faith is tested. Did the small test come round again, and did you pause before choosing? Day five hundred twenty-nine.

Early morning, after a damp night, you can see them everywhere. Webs strung between fence posts, across the corners of windows, between the stems in the garden, each one beaded with dew, catching the light. They're beautiful, and a spider worked hard on each one. And then you walk through one without seeing it, and it's gone, a few strands on your sleeve. Surah Al-'Ankabut is named for that web, and for one verse that uses it as a picture.

The verse is a parable. Pickthall: "The likeness of those who choose other patrons than Allah is as the likeness of the spider when she taketh unto herself a house, and lo! the frailest of all houses is the spider's house, if they but knew." Three things to notice. First, the word patrons: awliya', protectors, the ones you lean on. The verse is about where people put their weight. Second, the spider isn't lazy or foolish. She builds. She works hard, and what she builds is intricate and real. It's just that as shelter it can't hold. It keeps out nothing: not rain, not wind, not a careless hand. Third, the ending: if they but knew. As if the people leaning on the wrong thing could see it, if they looked. The surah tells of several peoples before this verse, Nuh's, Ibrahim's, Lut's, 'Ad, Thamud, Qarun, Pharaoh, who trusted in their strength, their wealth, their idols, and found it was thread. There's also a story often told about a spider, from the Prophet's journey to Medina: that when he and Abu Bakr hid in the cave of Thawr, a spider spun a web across the entrance, and the pursuers passed by. That's a story people tell, and its chains are weak; the Qur'an mentions the cave but not the spider. So the same creature appears in two pictures. In the verse, the web is the frailest of houses. In the story, a frail web, held by God, protects. What matters, in both, is who you lean on.
screen: `OTHER PATRONS: WHAT YOU LEAN ON.` · `SHE BUILDS, AND IT CAN'T HOLD.` · `IF THEY BUT KNEW.` · `THE WEB AT THE CAVE: A STORY TOLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice something you lean on that's thin. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think about what you reach for when things wobble. Your phone. Someone's approval. A balance in an account. Being busy. Being right. These aren't bad in themselves; the spider's silk isn't bad either. But pick one and ask, honestly: if the wind came, would this hold me? Then ask what would. If you pray, you can lean your weight, for this minute, on God. The bell holds the time.
The spider's house. The Qur'an's picture of leaning on anything other than God: carefully built, beautiful, and the frailest of all houses. Today's word.
Your line: not the spider's house. Today, the next time you reach for the thin thing you noticed, stop and take one steady breath first. Day five hundred twenty-nine.

530.title: Defeated, then victorious
530.hook: the Romans have been defeated, and within a few years will win (30:2–4)
530.howItsDone: Muslims read the opening of Surah Ar-Rum as a prophecy fulfilled in the Byzantine recovery under Heraclius, and as a reminder that the outcome of events belongs to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the spider's house, and your line was not the spider's house. What thin thing did you catch yourself reaching for? Day five hundred thirty, and a new surah.

News of a far-off war reaches Mecca. Two empires are fighting: the Romans of Constantinople, whom historians now call the Byzantines, and the Persians. And the Romans are losing. In Mecca, far from the fighting, people take sides. A report in Tirmidhi says the Muslims wanted the Romans to win, since they were people of a scripture, and the Quraysh wanted the Persians to win, since the Persians, like them, had no scripture. And then a surah opens with a headline.

Surah Ar-Rum, the Romans, the thirtieth. Pickthall: "The Romans have been defeated". In the nearer land, the verses go on, and after their defeat they will be victorious, within a few years. The phrase is bid' sinin. Bid' in Arabic means a handful, a small number; the same report in Tirmidhi gives it as between three and nine. And then: on that day the believers will rejoice in God's help. The Quraysh laughed at it. The report says Abu Bakr was so sure that he made a wager with some of them, before wagers like that were forbidden, and when the Romans won, he won it. Tradition says the emperor Heraclius turned the war. Some commentators link the believers' rejoicing to the same season as their own victory at Badr; others read it differently, and scholars have discussed exactly which events fit. But the verses don't stay with empires. The very next lines say: God's is the command, before and after. And then the surah widens out into a long meditation on signs: night and day, rain on dead earth, the cycle of life. In the surah's picture, a defeat isn't the end of a story. It's a chapter. The defeated can win, within a handful of years, and the One who turns it is the One who brings green out of dead ground.
screen: `THE ROMANS HAVE BEEN DEFEATED.` · `BID' SININ: A HANDFUL OF YEARS.` · `ABU BAKR'S WAGER.` · `GOD'S IS THE COMMAND, BEFORE AND AFTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hope in a reversal. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of one place in your life where you're losing right now. A fight with your health, a project that keeps failing, a relationship that's gone cold, a habit that keeps winning. Don't pretend it isn't a defeat. Just hold it, and then let yourself imagine the same scene a handful of years from now, turned around. What would be different? What small step points that way? If you pray, you can ask for help with it. The bell holds the time.
Defeated. The opening of Ar-Rum: the Romans have been defeated, and after their defeat they will win, within a handful of years. Today's word.
Your line: within a few years. Today, take the small step you pictured toward the reversal, even if it's tiny. Day five hundred thirty.

531.title: Love and mercy between you
531.hook: He made mates for you to find rest in, and put love and mercy between you (30:21)
531.howItsDone: 30:21 is widely recited at Muslim weddings and written on wedding cards and gifts, and Muslims often describe marriage through its words: rest, love and mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Romans defeated, and your line was within a few years. What tiny step did you take toward a reversal? Day five hundred thirty-one.

At many Muslim weddings, at some point, someone reads one particular verse. You'll often find it on the invitation too, in Arabic calligraphy, sometimes in gold. Plenty of people know this line without knowing much else of Surah Ar-Rum. It's short. It comes in the middle of a list of God's signs, between the creation of human beings from dust and the creation of the heavens and earth. And it puts a marriage, an ordinary household, right there among them.

Pickthall: "And of His signs is this: He created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy." Then: in that are signs for people who reflect. Start with from yourselves. Not from some other substance; of the same kind, the same nature. Then the purpose: li-taskunu ilayha, that you might find rest in them. The root s-k-n means stillness, settling, dwelling. The same root gives sakina, tranquility, and maskan, a home. So a spouse is described as somewhere you come to rest, the way you come home. Then two words, carefully chosen. Mawadda, love, warm affection, the kind you can see. And rahma, mercy, from the same root as the womb, as ar-Rahman. Commentators have enjoyed setting the two side by side. Some say mawadda is the love of the early years, and rahma is what carries a couple when looks fade and someone gets ill. Others say mawadda is love you feel, and rahma is care you choose, even on days the feeling is thin. Either way, the verse doesn't stop at love. It adds mercy, as if it knows love alone won't always be enough. And the verse says God put them there, ja'ala baynakum. Not you made them. He placed them between you. Many Muslims hear it as a reason for gratitude, and as a standard. A hadith in Tirmidhi says the best of you are those who are best to their families. The Qur'an counts a quiet kitchen, two people at rest with each other, as a sign as real as the sky.
screen: `HELPMEETS FROM YOURSELVES.` · `SAKAN: A PLACE TO COME TO REST.` · `MAWADDA, AND THEN RAHMA.` · `HE PUT THEM BETWEEN YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: show love to someone close. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of the person you come home to, or the one you'd most like to: a spouse, a parent, a sibling, a friend, a child. Picture their face at the end of an ordinary day. Ask yourself where your love for them is easy right now, and where it needs mercy instead. Decide on one thing you'll do for them today. Not a grand gesture. Tea made the way they like it. An apology. A long hug. If you pray, you can thank God for them by name. The bell holds the time.
Love and mercy between you. Mawadda and rahma, which Ar-Rum says God placed between spouses, so they could find rest in one another. Today's word.
screen: `LOVE AND MERCY BETWEEN YOU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: love and mercy between. Today, do the small thing you chose for the person close to you, before the evening ends. Day five hundred thirty-one.

532.title: Tongues and colors
532.hook: the diversity of your languages and colors is among His signs (30:22)
532.howItsDone: Muslims often cite 30:22, 49:13 and the Prophet's farewell sermon to teach that no language, people or color is above another, and that only taqwa distinguishes people before God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mawadda and rahma, and your line was love and mercy between. Who did you do the small thing for, and how did they take it? Day five hundred thirty-two, the end of the week.

Stand in the courtyard of the Great Mosque in Mecca at any hour, and listen. Indonesian, Urdu, Turkish, Hausa, Bosnian, Malay, Bengali, Somali, French, English, Arabic in a dozen accents. Faces of every shade, from every continent, walking the same circle, many in the same white cloth. Some pilgrims come home talking less about the buildings than about the crowd. The verse right after yesterday's has a word for what they saw.

Pickthall: "And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours. Lo! herein indeed are portents for men of knowledge." Look at the company the verse keeps. The heavens, the earth, and then, in the same breath, the fact that people speak differently and look different. Human variety is put on the same shelf as the sky. Not a problem to be solved, and not a ranking. A sign, an aya, the same word used for a verse of the Qur'an. And who is meant to read this sign? Men of knowledge, in Pickthall's English; in Arabic, al-'alimin, those who know. As if the more you learn about people, the more there is to see. The Qur'an says something close in Surah Al-Hujurat: We made you nations and tribes so that you might know one another, and the noblest of you with God is the most mindful of Him. And in the sermon the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ gave at his farewell pilgrimage, reported in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, he said an Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor a non-Arab over an Arab, nor a light-skinned person over a dark-skinned one, nor the reverse, except by taqwa. His first community already looked like that: Bilal from Abyssinia, Salman from Persia, Suhayb, called the Roman. This week ran from Al-Qasas through Al-'Ankabut to Ar-Rum: strong and trustworthy, do good as good was done, faith is tested, not the spider's house, within a few years, love and mercy between. And today, the widest one: difference is a sign.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn a greeting in another language. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of someone you see often whose first language isn't yours. A neighbor, a colleague, the person who runs the corner shop, a classmate's parent. What language do they speak at home? Decide to learn how to say hello, or thank you, in it. Picture saying it to them, a little clumsily, and seeing their face change. If you pray, you can thank God for one person whose difference has taught you something. The bell holds the time.
Tongues and colors. Ar-Rum counts the variety of human languages and colors among God's signs, beside the heavens and the earth. Today's word.
Your line: difference is a sign. Today, use the greeting you learned, even if you get it a bit wrong. Day five hundred thirty-two.
